questions.explanation: 'Since March' marks a period continuing to the present, which requires the present perfect. The simple past 'rose' would describe a completed event rather than an ongoing trend.

questions.stem: It is essential that every officer ___ the security briefing before departure.
choices: attends
attend
will attend
attended
questions.explanation: 'It is essential that' triggers the subjunctive, which takes the bare infinitive regardless of subject. The same construction governs 'it is imperative that he be present' and 'we ask that she remain.'

questions.stem: The delegation could not agree on ___ should lead the working group.
choices: who
whom
which
whomever
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the subject of 'should lead' within the noun clause; the preposition 'on' governs the entire clause rather than the pronoun alone. Substituting 'he should lead' confirms the subjective case.

questions.stem: Each of the three sections ___ submitted its portion of the report.
choices: were
has
have
are
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb is 'has'; the intervening 'of the three sections' does not change the subject's number. The singular 'its' later in the sentence confirms the agreement.

questions.stem: Were the treaty ___ today, ratification would still take months.
choices: signing
signed
sign
signs
questions.explanation: The inverted 'were... signed' is a present counterfactual requiring the past participle, paired with 'would' in the result clause. This construction is the formal equivalent of 'if the treaty were signed today.'

questions.stem: The report was more thorough than ___ the previous year.
choices: they
them
it was
those
questions.explanation: The comparison is between two reports, so the second term needs a matching singular clause. 'Them' and 'those' are plural and would have no antecedent in the sentence.

questions.stem: Neither of the two proposals ___ the committee's stated criteria.
choices: have met
meet
meets
are meeting
questions.explanation: 'Neither' used as a pronoun is singular and takes 'meets.' The plural 'proposals' inside the prepositional phrase is a distractor rather than the subject.

questions.stem: The ambassador spoke to the press ___ than her predecessor had.
choices: more frequently
most frequently
frequenter
more frequent
questions.explanation: The word modifies the verb 'spoke,' so it must be an adverb, and a two-item comparison requires the comparative rather than the superlative form.

questions.stem: The officer, along with several colleagues, ___ been reassigned.
choices: are
were
has
have
questions.explanation: 'Along with' is parenthetical, leaving 'officer' as the singular subject. The pattern matches 'together with,' 'as well as,' and 'in addition to' — none of which compound the subject.

questions.stem: The committee will announce ___ decision on Friday.
choices: its
there
it's
their
questions.explanation: 'Committee' is a collective noun taking singular agreement in American usage, so the possessive is 'its.' British usage often prefers 'their,' but the FSOT follows American conventions.

questions.stem: The analyst recommended that the finding ___ withheld pending verification.
choices: would be
is
was
be
questions.explanation: 'Recommend that' takes the subjunctive, using the bare infinitive 'be.' Verbs of demanding, insisting, proposing, and requiring all govern this construction.

questions.stem: Statistics on migration ___ published annually by the department.
choices: are
was
has been
is
questions.explanation: Here 'statistics' means numerical data and takes a plural verb. The word is singular only when it names the academic discipline, as in 'statistics is a demanding field.'

questions.stem: By the end of next month, the section ___ every pending case.
choices: will process
would process
will have processed
has processed
questions.explanation: An action completed before a specified future point takes the future perfect. 'Will process' would place the action at that time rather than before it.

questions.stem: The two governments settled the dispute ___ themselves without mediation.
choices: among
between
within
amongst
questions.explanation: 'Between' governs two parties; 'among' is used for three or more. The distinction is worth preserving because it silently tells the reader how many parties are involved.

questions.stem: Not only ___ the deadline missed, but the revised text was also incomplete.
choices: the section was
was the section
the section
had the section
questions.explanation: A sentence opening with 'not only' requires subject-verb inversion in that clause. The uninverted 'not only the section was' is a common error in otherwise careful writing.

questions.stem: The findings were shared with the ambassador and ___.
choices: myself
mine
I
me
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of the preposition 'with,' so the objective 'me' is required. 'Myself' is reflexive and needs an antecedent in the same clause, which this sentence does not supply.

questions.stem: The cable, which ___ drafted overnight, reached Washington by morning.
choices: were
have been
are
was
questions.explanation: 'Which' refers to the singular 'cable,' so the verb is singular. Relative pronouns take the number of their antecedent, not of any nearer noun.

questions.stem: The number of pending applications ___ fallen sharply.
choices: has
were
have
are
questions.explanation: 'The number of' is singular; 'a number of' is plural. The difference turns entirely on the article, which is why the pair is worth memorizing rather than reasoning through.

questions.stem: Had the section anticipated the surge, additional staff ___ requested earlier.
choices: would be
had been
will have been
would have been
questions.explanation: The inverted 'had the section anticipated' is a past counterfactual, so the result clause takes 'would have been.' 'Would be' belongs to a present or future counterfactual.

questions.stem: The policy affects everyone ___ holds a diplomatic passport.
choices: who
which
whose
whom
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the subject of 'holds' in the relative clause. A quick test is substitution: 'he holds a diplomatic passport' takes the subjective form.

questions.stem: The delegation had hoped to have completed the review, but the schedule ___ it impossible.
choices: make
made
makes
had made
questions.explanation: The main clause is in the past ('had hoped'), so the coordinated clause takes the simple past 'made.' The past perfect 'had made' would place the schedule's effect before the hoping, reversing the sequence.

questions.stem: Politics ___ an unavoidable element of every posting.
choices: have been
were
is
are
questions.explanation: 'Politics' takes a singular verb when it denotes the general subject or activity. It is plural only in constructions like 'his politics are unclear,' where it means someone's particular views.

questions.stem: The report identified three risks, ___ of which had been anticipated.
choices: nothing
no one
none
neither
questions.explanation: 'None of which' is the correct partitive with three items. 'Neither' applies only to exactly two, and 'no one' and 'nothing' cannot take the 'of which' construction.

questions.stem: The consul general, together with the section chiefs, ___ the visiting delegation.
choices: are greeting
greet
have greeted
greets
questions.explanation: 'Together with' does not compound the subject, so the singular 'consul general' governs the verb. Replacing the phrase with a comma-free reading makes the agreement obvious.

questions.stem: If the department ___ more transparent, public confidence might improve.
choices: was
is
had been
were
questions.explanation: A present hypothetical contrary to fact takes the subjunctive 'were' regardless of subject number, paired with 'might' in the result clause. 'Was' would state a past fact rather than a hypothetical.

questions.stem: Every one of the recommendations ___ been implemented.
choices: were
has
are
have
questions.explanation: 'Every one' singles out individual items and is singular. Note the two-word spelling: 'everyone' as one word refers to people and would not fit this sentence.

questions.stem: The section chief prefers that reporting cables ___ concise.
choices: be
will be
are
were
questions.explanation: 'Prefer that' belongs to the family of verbs governing the subjunctive, which uses the bare infinitive. The indicative 'are' would report a fact rather than express a preference.

questions.stem: The embassy has fewer local staff ___ it did a decade ago.
choices: then
as
that
than
questions.explanation: 'Than' introduces the second term of a comparison; 'then' marks sequence in time. The pair is among the most frequently confused in written English precisely because they are near-homophones.

questions.stem: The delegates, most of ___ had traveled overnight, requested a later start.
choices: who
whom
them
which
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is the object of the preposition 'of.' 'Them' would create a comma splice by making the clause independent, and 'which' cannot refer to people.

questions.stem: The department's response had little ___ on the outcome of the talks.
choices: effect
affect
affective
effected
questions.explanation: A noun follows 'little,' and the noun form is 'effect.' 'Affect' is the ordinary verb meaning to influence; its noun use is confined to psychology.

questions.stem: The negotiator's position was ___ — she would not move regardless of the inducement offered.
choices: adamantine
adamant
ardent
arduous
questions.explanation: 'Adamant' means unyielding, which the clause after the dash defines. 'Arduous' means difficult and describes a task rather than a stance; 'ardent' means passionate, which is not the same as immovable.

questions.stem: The two accounts of the meeting were largely ___, differing only in minor details.
choices: consequent
constant
consonant
consistent
questions.explanation: 'Consistent' means free of contradiction, which the second clause confirms. 'Consonant' can mean in agreement but is used of things harmonizing with a principle rather than of two accounts matching.

questions.stem: The ambassador sought to ___ concerns that the policy signaled a broader shift.
choices: allay
alley
alloy
ally
questions.explanation: 'Allay' means to reduce or calm, and 'allay concerns' is the standard collocation. The other three are unrelated words that happen to be near-homophones.

questions.stem: The agreement will ___ the existing memorandum of understanding.
choices: suspend
surpass
supersede
supercede
questions.explanation: 'Supersede' means to replace and take the place of; note the -sede ending, which is unique to this word in English. 'Surpass' means to exceed in degree, which is not what a replacing instrument does.

questions.stem: The proposal was rejected on ___ grounds rather than for any substantive objection.
choices: procedural
proceeding
preceding
precedential
questions.explanation: 'Procedural' refers to process, which the sentence contrasts with substance. 'Precedential' means establishing a precedent — a different concept that would not stand in opposition to substantive.

questions.stem: The delegation's arrival was ___ by fog at the airport.
choices: deluged
deluded
delayed
diluted
questions.explanation: 'Delayed' means postponed, which fog plainly causes. The other options — deceived, weakened by dilution, and flooded — are near-homophones with unrelated meanings.

questions.stem: The report drew a clear ___ between advocacy and analysis.
choices: discretion
distinctive
distraction
distinction
questions.explanation: 'Draw a distinction' is the fixed idiom for marking a difference. 'Distinctive' is an adjective and cannot serve as the object of 'drew.'

questions.stem: The officer was asked to ___ the substance of a lengthy report for the ambassador.
choices: surmise
summon
sublimate
summarize
questions.explanation: 'Summarize' means to state concisely. 'Surmise' means to guess without evidence — the reverse of what a summary should do, which makes it the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.stem: The minister's remarks were ___ enough to satisfy both factions.
choices: equivalent
equivocal
equitable
unequivocal
questions.explanation: 'Equivocal' means open to more than one interpretation, which is what permits both factions to be satisfied. 'Unequivocal' means precisely the opposite and would have forced a choice between them.

questions.stem: The two departments operate under ___ mandates that occasionally overlap.
choices: discretionary
descriptive
discrete
discreet
questions.explanation: 'Discrete' means separate and distinct. 'Discreet' means careful about revealing information — the two are homophones, and this pair appears on virtually every usage list.

questions.stem: The consul was praised for her ___ in handling a sensitive family matter.
choices: discreet
decorated
decorous
discrete
questions.explanation: Here the sense required is careful about disclosure, which is 'discreet.' This item is the deliberate mirror of the preceding one — the same homophone pair, with the other member correct.

questions.stem: The new procedures are expected to ___ processing times considerably.
choices: seduce
induce
deduce
reduce
questions.explanation: 'Reduce' means to decrease, which fits processing times. 'Deduce' means to infer from evidence and 'induce' to bring about — both plausible-looking but semantically wrong here.

questions.stem: The evidence was ___ to the question before the panel and was therefore excluded.
choices: irreparable
irreverent
irrelevant
irresolute
questions.explanation: 'Irrelevant' means not bearing on the matter, which is why evidence would be excluded. 'Irreverent' means disrespectful — a different word entirely that is nonetheless a frequent substitution error.

questions.stem: The mission's staffing has been ___ reduced over three budget cycles.
choices: gradation
graduated
gradually
gradual
questions.explanation: The word modifies the verb phrase 'has been reduced' and must be an adverb. 'Graduated' would suggest reduction in defined steps, a claim the sentence does not make.

questions.stem: The commission's findings ___ the earlier account rather than confirming it.
choices: contrasted
contravened
contradicted
contraindicated
questions.explanation: 'Contradicted' means asserted the opposite of, which the sentence sets against confirming. 'Contravened' means violated a rule or law and takes rules rather than accounts as its object.

questions.stem: She was appointed to the post ___ of her predecessor's resignation.
choices: because
in light
as a result
on account
questions.explanation: 'On account of' is the complete idiomatic phrase. 'Because' requires 'because of' before a noun phrase, and 'as a result' and 'in light' would need 'of' plus different phrasing to work.

questions.stem: The delegation's proposal represented a ___ improvement over the previous draft.
choices: markedly
remarked
marking
marked
questions.explanation: 'Marked' as an adjective means noticeable or pronounced. 'Markedly' is the adverb and cannot modify the noun 'improvement.'

questions.stem: The officer's conduct was entirely ___ with department regulations.
choices: complacent
compliant
complaint
complicit
questions.explanation: 'Compliant' means conforming to rules. 'Complaint' is a noun differing by one transposed letter, and 'complacent' means self-satisfied — both are common typing and reading slips.

questions.stem: The two positions are not merely different but ___.
choices: incomprehensible
incomparable
incontrovertible
incompatible
questions.explanation: 'Incompatible' means unable to coexist, which is the escalation from mere difference the sentence sets up. 'Incomparable' means without equal — a compliment rather than a statement of conflict.

questions.stem: The department declined to ___ on the pending investigation.
choices: commit
commence
comment
commend
questions.explanation: 'Comment on' is the idiom for offering remarks about a subject. 'Commend' means to praise and 'commence' to begin — both near-homographs with entirely different meanings.

questions.stem: The provision was included at the ___ of the smaller delegations.
choices: bequest
beset
behest
behalf
questions.explanation: 'At the behest of' means at the request or urging of. 'Bequest' is a gift left in a will, and 'on behalf of' — a different preposition — means acting for someone rather than at their request.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly joins the two independent clauses?
choices: The talks resumed in March, however they collapsed again in June.
The talks resumed in March they collapsed again in June.
The talks resumed in March; they collapsed again in June.
The talks resumed in March, they collapsed again in June.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses without a conjunction. The first and fourth are comma splices — 'however' is a conjunctive adverb and cannot join clauses with only a comma before it.

questions.stem: Which sentence corrects the dangling modifier in 'Having reviewed the evidence, the conclusion seemed inescapable.'?
choices: Having reviewed the evidence, the panel found the conclusion inescapable.
Having reviewed the evidence, the conclusion was inescapable to the panel.
Having been reviewed, the evidence made the conclusion inescapable.
The conclusion, having reviewed the evidence, seemed inescapable.
questions.explanation: The participial phrase must modify the subject of the main clause, and only the panel can have reviewed evidence. Options {{1,3}} leave 'conclusion' as the reviewer, and the fourth changes the meaning by making the evidence the actor.

questions.stem: Which sentence keeps all three items in the series parallel?
choices: The post is responsible for issuing visas, for consular protection, and reporting on politics.
The post is responsible for issuing visas, providing consular protection, and reporting on politics.
The post is responsible for visa issuance, to provide consular protection, and reporting.
The post issues visas, consular protection, and political reporting.
questions.explanation: Three gerund phrases after a single 'for' produce a clean parallel series. Option {{3}} is not merely unparallel but ungrammatical, since a post cannot 'issue' consular protection.

questions.stem: Which sentence compares the two workloads correctly?
choices: The consular section's workload is heavier than the political section is.
Compared to the political section, the consular workload is heavier than it.
The workload of the consular section is heavier than that of the political section.
The workload of the consular section is heavier than the political section.
questions.explanation: 'That of' makes the second term a workload rather than a section, so like is compared with like. Option {{3}} compares a workload to a section, and the fourth is simply ungrammatical.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates the introductory clause?
choices: Although the deadline had passed, the application was accepted.
Although the deadline had passed the application was accepted.
Although the deadline had passed; the application was accepted.
Although, the deadline had passed, the application was accepted.
questions.explanation: A subordinate clause preceding the main clause takes a comma after it. A semicolon cannot follow a dependent clause, and the comma after 'although' in option {{3}} separates the conjunction from its own clause.

questions.stem: Which revision best repairs 'The report which was commissioned last year and that has still not been released is now overdue.'?
choices: The report which was commissioned last year, and that has still not been released is now overdue.
The report, commissioned last year, and that has still not been released, is overdue.
The report that was commissioned last year and which has still not been released is now overdue.
The report, which was commissioned last year and has still not been released, is now overdue.
questions.explanation: One relative pronoun governs both verbs, and paired commas set off the nonrestrictive clause. Mixing 'which' and 'that' for coordinated clauses, as the original and option {{2}} do, breaks the parallel.

questions.stem: Which sentence places 'nearly' correctly to mean that the total approached one thousand?
choices: The section processed one thousand nearly cases.
Nearly the section processed one thousand cases.
The section processed nearly one thousand cases.
The section nearly processed one thousand cases.
questions.explanation: 'Nearly' must sit immediately before the quantity it limits. Option {{3}} modifies the verb and implies the section came close to processing but did not — a genuinely different claim.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses correlative conjunctions?
choices: The delegation not only accepted the text nor proposed an alternative.
The delegation neither accepted the text or proposed an alternative.
The delegation neither accepted the text nor did they propose an alternative.
The delegation neither accepted the text nor proposed an alternative.
questions.explanation: 'Neither...nor' must be followed by grammatically parallel elements — here two past-tense verbs. 'Neither' pairs only with 'nor,' which rules out option {{1}}, and the fourth mismatches 'not only' with 'nor.'

questions.stem: Which sentence is free of a run-on?
choices: The minister arrived late the meeting had already begun.
The minister arrived, late the meeting had already begun.
The minister arrived late; the meeting had already begun.
The minister arrived late the meeting, had already begun.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses require a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus coordinating conjunction. Options {{1,3}} merely relocate the comma without addressing the fusion.

questions.stem: Which revision is most concise while preserving the meaning of 'It is the recommendation of the working group that the deadline be extended.'?
choices: An extension of the deadline is what the working group recommends.
The recommendation of the working group is for an extension of the deadline.
The working group recommends extending the deadline.
It is recommended by the working group that the deadline be extended.
questions.explanation: Six words replace fourteen by naming the actor and converting the nominalization 'recommendation' back into the verb 'recommends.' The other options preserve either the passive or the nominalization.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
choices: The mission has: three priorities, security, prosperity, and values.
The mission has three priorities, security: prosperity and values.
The three priorities are: security, prosperity, and values.
The mission has three priorities: security, prosperity, and values.
questions.explanation: A colon must follow a complete independent clause. Option {{2}} breaks the clause between the linking verb and its complement, a very common error in lists introduced by 'are' or 'include.'

questions.stem: Which sentence resolves the ambiguous pronoun reference?
choices: The department briefed the embassy and it released a statement.
When the department briefed the embassy, they released a statement.
When the department briefed the embassy, it released a statement.
After briefing the embassy, the department released a statement.
questions.explanation: Recasting the first clause as a participial phrase eliminates the second noun entirely, so only the department can be the subject. Any version retaining both nouns leaves 'it' or 'they' genuinely ambiguous.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly handles the series with internal commas?
choices: The delegation visited Lima, Peru, Quito, Ecuador, and Bogotá, Colombia.
The delegation visited Lima Peru, Quito Ecuador, and Bogotá Colombia.
The delegation visited: Lima, Peru, Quito, Ecuador, Bogotá, Colombia.
The delegation visited Lima, Peru; Quito, Ecuador; and Bogotá, Colombia.
questions.explanation: When list items themselves contain commas, semicolons separate the items. Option {{0}} produces a six-item list in which no reader can tell cities from countries.

questions.stem: Which sentence corrects the fragment 'While the negotiations continued through the night.'?
choices: The negotiations continued through the night. While no agreement was reached.
While the negotiations continued through the night, no agreement was reached.
While the negotiations continued through the night; no agreement was reached.
While, the negotiations continued through the night, no agreement was reached.
questions.explanation: The subordinating conjunction 'while' makes the clause dependent, so it must attach to an independent clause with a comma. Option {{0}} relocates the fragment rather than repairing it.

questions.stem: Which sentence maintains a consistent voice?
choices: The section drafted the cable, and the front office cleared it.
The cable was drafted by the section and the front office cleared it.
The cable was drafted by the section, and clearance was given by the front office, which was expected.
Drafting was by the section; clearance, the front office.
questions.explanation: Two active clauses with parallel structure read most directly. The first shifts from passive to active mid-sentence, and the fourth omits the verbs entirely in a telegraphic style unsuited to formal prose.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses paired dashes?
choices: Two issues, funding and staffing — remain unresolved.
Two issues—funding and staffing—remain, unresolved.
Two issues — funding and staffing, remain unresolved.
Two issues — funding and staffing — remain unresolved.
questions.explanation: Dashes setting off an interruption must be paired. Mixing a dash with a comma leaves the interruption unbalanced, and option {{1}} adds a comma that severs the verb from its complement.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids the comma splice?
choices: The vote failed, three members, abstained.
The vote failed, therefore three members abstained.
The vote failed, three members abstained.
The vote failed because three members abstained.
questions.explanation: Subordinating with 'because' makes the second clause dependent and states the causal relation. Option {{1}} both splices and reverses the causation, since the abstentions caused the failure rather than the reverse.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly subordinates the less important idea?
choices: Although the report identified a serious vulnerability, it was late.
Although it was late, the report identified a serious vulnerability.
The report was late, and it identified a serious vulnerability.
The report identified a serious vulnerability, and it was late.
questions.explanation: Subordination signals relative importance: placing the lateness in the dependent clause foregrounds the vulnerability. Option {{0}} inverts the emphasis, implying that lateness is the more significant fact.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
choices: The officer who drafted the memorandum has since departed post.
The officer who drafted the memorandum, has since departed post.
The officer, who drafted the memorandum; has since departed post.
The officer, who drafted the memorandum has since departed post.
questions.explanation: The clause identifies which officer, making it restrictive and therefore unpunctuated. Options {{1,3}} supply only one comma, stranding the clause and separating the subject from its verb.

questions.stem: Which revision eliminates the redundancy in 'The two sides mutually agreed to jointly cooperate on the joint initiative.'?
choices: The two sides jointly agreed to cooperate on the joint initiative.
Both sides mutually agreed to jointly cooperate.
The two sides agreed to cooperate on the initiative.
The two sides mutually agreed to cooperate on the initiative.
questions.explanation: Agreement between two sides is already mutual, cooperation is already joint, and repeating 'joint' before 'initiative' compounds it. Only option {{2}} removes all three redundancies.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly places the modifying phrase?
choices: The officer submitted the report that had been revised twice to the ambassador.
The officer submitted the report to the ambassador that had been revised twice.
Revised twice, the officer submitted the report to the ambassador.
The officer submitted to the ambassador the report that had been revised twice.
questions.explanation: The relative clause must sit next to 'report,' which options {{0,3}} both achieve — but the third reads more naturally, keeping subject, verb, and object in order. The first attaches the revisions to the ambassador and the fourth to the officer.

questions.stem: Which sentence best combines 'The embassy requested additional staff. The request was denied. The backlog grew.'?
choices: The embassy requested additional staff and the request was denied and the backlog grew.
The embassy requested additional staff; the request was denied; the backlog grew.
After the embassy's request for additional staff was denied, the backlog grew.
The embassy requested additional staff, the request was denied, and the backlog grew.
questions.explanation: Subordinating the first two facts into a single clause makes the causal sequence explicit and puts the consequence in the main clause. The other options merely string coordinate clauses together without indicating how they relate.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
choices: The three ambassadors residence's were renovated.
The three ambassadors's residences were renovated.
The three ambassadors' residences were renovated.
The three ambassador's residences were renovated.
questions.explanation: A plural noun ending in -s takes an apostrophe after the s. Option {{3}} is a singular possessive, which contradicts 'three,' and the remaining options misplace or double the marker.

questions.stem: Which transition best fits? 'The agreement was signed in April. ___, implementing legislation has not been introduced.'
choices: Consequently
Therefore
As a result
To date
questions.explanation: The second sentence reports what has not yet happened, so a time-marking transition fits. The other three assert that the absence of legislation followed logically from the signing, which reverses the relationship.

questions.stem: Four sentences form a paragraph. Which should come second? (1) The department has since issued revised guidance. (2) Officers at three posts applied the standard inconsistently. (3) An internal review found the original guidance ambiguous. (4) Applicants in similar circumstances received different outcomes.
choices: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the problem and sentence 4 gives its immediate consequence, which must precede the review that diagnosed the cause and the guidance that resolved it. Sentence 1's 'since' marks it as last.

questions.stem: Which version states the condition most economically?
choices: Should it be the case that the deadline is missed, an extension may be requested.
In the event that the deadline is missed, an extension may be requested.
In those circumstances where the deadline happens to be missed, an extension may be requested.
If the deadline is missed, an extension may be requested.
questions.explanation: 'If' does in one word what the other openings take four to eight words to do. Phrases like 'in the event that' and 'should it be the case that' are the standard padding of official prose.

questions.stem: A paragraph argues that the visa backlog resulted from staffing rather than demand. Which sentence does NOT belong?
choices: Application volume was within two percent of the prior year's.
The section's interview capacity fell by roughly a third.
Six adjudicator positions remained vacant for eleven months.
Neighboring posts introduced online appointment scheduling.
questions.explanation: What other posts did with scheduling bears on neither staffing nor demand at this post. The other three each support the argument — flat demand, vacant positions, and reduced capacity.

questions.stem: Which transition best fits? 'Most member states supported the proposal. ___, two of the largest contributors opposed it.'
choices: Similarly
Furthermore
However
Accordingly
questions.explanation: The second sentence introduces a significant exception, requiring a contrastive transition. 'Similarly' and 'furthermore' both signal continuity, and 'accordingly' asserts consequence.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best open a paragraph whose remaining sentences describe three obstacles to ratification?
choices: Three obstacles stand between the signed text and ratification.
The treaty was signed in Geneva last March.
Similar treaties have been ratified within eighteen months.
Ratification requires a two-thirds vote of the Senate.
questions.explanation: A topic sentence should announce both the subject and the structure of what follows. The other options supply background or comparison that the paragraph, as described, does not go on to develop.

questions.stem: Which revision is clearest? 'There are three factors which are responsible for the delay that has occurred.'
choices: There are three factors that are responsible for the delay.
The delay that occurred was caused by three factors that were responsible.
Three factors are what caused the delay to occur.
Three factors caused the delay.
questions.explanation: Five words replace thirteen by cutting the empty 'there are' opening, the relative clause, and the redundant 'that has occurred.' The other options keep at least one of the three.

questions.stem: Which sentence best concludes a paragraph arguing that a sanctions regime achieved its stated aim?
choices: The regime was renewed for a further two years.
Sanctions have been used against many countries.
The target government reversed the policy within nine months of designation.
Sanctions impose costs on civilian populations.
questions.explanation: A concluding sentence should deliver the evidence that settles the paragraph's claim, and a policy reversal is precisely what 'achieved its aim' means. Renewal is ambiguous and could as easily indicate failure.

questions.stem: Which transition best fits? 'The pilot reduced processing times at every participating post. ___, the department plans to extend it nationwide.'
choices: Nevertheless
Although
Conversely
Accordingly
questions.explanation: Extension follows logically from success, so a consequential transition is required. 'Nevertheless' and 'conversely' both signal contrast, and 'although' is a subordinating conjunction that cannot open a sentence in this position.

questions.stem: Which revision most improves clarity? 'It was determined by the review board that the applicant's eligibility was not able to be established.'
choices: It was determined that the applicant could not establish eligibility by the board.
Eligibility was not able to be established, the review board determined.
The review board determined that eligibility could not be established.
The determination of the review board was that eligibility was not establishable.
questions.explanation: Naming the actor, using an active verb, and replacing 'was not able to be established' with 'could not be established' halves the length. The other options preserve the passive, the nominalization, or both.

questions.stem: In a paragraph explaining why a post exceeded its budget, which sentence is least relevant?
choices: Two unplanned high-level visits required additional support.
The post's residence was built in 1968.
Local currency depreciation raised the dollar cost of contracts.
Emergency evacuation costs were not foreseen in the original request.
questions.explanation: The construction date bears no evident relation to a budget overrun. The other three each identify an unanticipated cost — evacuation, exchange rate movement, and visit support.

questions.stem: Four sentences form a paragraph. Which should come first? (1) That assumption proved incorrect. (2) The forecast assumed commodity prices would remain stable. (3) Revenue fell 14 percent below projection. (4) Prices declined by nearly a third in the second quarter.
choices: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 states the assumption without depending on anything prior. Sentence 1's 'that assumption' points backward, and sentences 4 and 3 give the falsification and its consequence in turn.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids stacked negatives?
choices: It is not improbable that the delegation will fail to refuse the invitation.
The delegation is not unlikely to not turn down the invitation.
The delegation will probably accept the invitation.
It is not unlikely that the delegation will not decline the invitation.
questions.explanation: Six words replace formulations requiring the reader to resolve two or three stacked negatives. Each distractor states the same thing while forcing the reader to track 'not,' 'un-,' and 'decline' simultaneously.

questions.stem: Which transition best fits? 'The two delegations reached agreement on tariffs. ___, the question of agricultural subsidies remains open.'
choices: Likewise
Consequently
Hence
That said
questions.explanation: The sentence qualifies the preceding success by naming what remains unresolved, which calls for a concessive transition. The other three all assert that the open question follows from the agreement.
